transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-03-30
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~38 minutes
Attendees: Max Chen (Redwood AE), Sara Patel (Redwood SE), Diego Morales (Redwood CSM), Liam O'Connor (Head of ML, StratoRide), Rita Bhatia (Engineering Manager), Tom Alvarez (Finance), Nina Song (SecOps)
Shared links: short pricing workbook (drive.redwood/stratoride-pilot), security pack (redwood.com/sec/soc2-kms.pdf)

Summary:
Quick intake to understand StratoRide's expected token volumes, latency targets and budget constraints for an in-app driver assistance model. Primary asks: per-token cost sensitivity, batching/caching levers to reduce burn, and options for VPC / private deployment if needed for residency. Agreed next step: 2-week pilot with perf run, Redwood to send pricing workbook and pilot config.

[00:00] Max: hey everyone thanks for joining, you all hear me ok?
[00:03] Liam: yep loud and clear, thanks Max. Rita and Tom from our side are on.
[00:06] Max: awesome, quick intros? I'll hand to Sara to do quick agenda.
[00:09] Sara: hi all, Sara Patel, SE at Redwood. Today we want to map your workload (qps, prompt sizes, latency targets), talk per-token economics and levers like batching, prefix cache, and quantization. then tradeoffs hosted vs dedicated vs private given your residency and security asks. then align on pilot scope.
[00:26] Rita: sounds good. Our immediate use-case is an in-app assistant for drivers — short prompts, lots of small generations (single-turn), peak at shift changes, maybe some multimodal later but not in scope now. Latency target ~200-300ms p95 for generate. Budget: we have a monthly cap for prod of roughly $35k to $50k to start — may scale later.
[00:48] Tom: from finance, we need clear unit economics and predictable burn. We can commit to reserved if the unit price is compelling.
[00:55] Sara: perfect, that helps. couple clarifying q's — what does a typical prompt look like and expected tokens out?
[01:02] Liam: prompts are short: driver state + intent like "Traffic slow near I-80, alternative route?" we typically see 8-25 tokens in, responses 20-60 tokens. avg roundtrip about 60 tokens.
[01:12] Max: so ballpark 60 tokens per request, high qps windows around 300-400 qps for ~15 minutes twice a day? is that right?
[01:19] Rita: yeah, peak windows approximate. daily active drivers ~50k, not all using assistant but initial pilot maybe 3k DAU.
[01:27] Sara: good — so pilot footprint we should size for ~3k active, peak qps ~150-200, average latency target 250ms. Now on per-token pricing: Redwood hosted is usage-based with published per-token tiers; dedicated is reserved GPU pools with lower per-token at higher commit and private adds infra + ops. Max, do you want to give a number example?
[01:50] Max: sure — rough example, hosted API for an open 7B-ish model we typically price at $0.0008 per input token and $0.0016 per output token in the public tiers (examples only). but with batching and prefix cache we see effective cost drop 20-50% depending on reuse. dedicated can reduce equivalent per-token cost further — down to ~40-60% of hosted depending on commit and model/quantization. private has higher fixed fees for the private control plane, but if you need VPC/KMS/residency that changes the trade.
[02:22] Tom: that's helpful; can you explain how batching gives you the drop? we're worried about latency impact.
[02:28] Sara: yes — two levers. dynamic request batching groups requests that arrive within a small window and uses GPU throughput better; this reduces per-token GPU time but adds a small queuing delay. Redwood's runtime can do micro-batching at 5-15ms windows for small sequences which often keeps p95 within your 250ms target. second is prefix/KV caching: for a lot of your prompts the driver context is repeated — if you cache the encoder states we avoid recomputing tokens, reducing work per request. that's very powerful for high reuse patterns.
[03:02] Liam: our prompts are fairly similar — driver profile + current telemetry — so prefix cache seems promising. what's the hit on memory?
[03:08] Sara: KV cache does consume memory per cached prefix per model shard; we can size the cache and evict LRU. it's a trade: bigger cache reduces recompute but needs dedicated capacity planning. for pilot we'll recommend baseline cache set to common prefixes (recent 100-200 contexts) and measure hit rate.
[03:26] Rita: can Redwood run the pilot on hosted first to prove the economics, then move to dedicated if it's cheaper?
[03:32] Max: that's a common path. hosted for quick time-to-value, run a perf+cost pilot, iterate on batching/cache, then if committed volumes justify reserved capacity we'll propose dedicated numbers.
[03:40] Nina: security question — we require KMS integration and audit logs; we may need customer-managed keys and VPC peering. Can Redwood support HSM-backed KMS and isolation?
[03:50] Sara: yes — Redwood Private supports customer KMS/HSM and a private control plane with VPC tunnels. Hosted has envelope encryption and optional BYOK integration for enterprise tiers. we'll share the SOC2 and KMS spec in the security pack link.
[04:03] Tom: does private change the per-token math? I mean the fixed costs will inflate but the per-token compute cost may be similar?
[04:11] Max: exactly. private introduces platform licensing and infra costs which are amortized over tokens. if your volume is high enough, amortized per-token cost on private can be attractive; for smaller pilots hosted or dedicated is usually better economics.
[04:22] Liam: can we talk numbers more concretely — with our expected 3k DAU and 60 tokens per request at 150 qps peak, what monthly burn ballpark?
[04:32] Sara: quick rough calc — assume 150 qps sustained for peak windows (2x15min/day), plus steady usage baseline ~10 qps off-peak. Let's be conservative and estimate 15M tokens/day -> that's ~450M tokens/month. At hosted blended $0.001 per token (simplified combined in+out), that's ~$450k/month — which is way over your stated budget. But that's naive; with caching/batching and model choice (smaller quantized 4-bit models) we can reduce effective tokens processed by caching and reduce per-token compute cost. With aggressive caching and batching we can often reach 60-70% reduction in token work for this workload; and dedicated reserved pricing could lower per-token from $0.001 to $0.0004. So pilot is needed to measure real hit rates.
[05:18] Tom: ok that's illuminating — we were thinking $35-50k — seems wide gap. so the goal of the pilot is to find ways to hit the budget or decide if we need to re-scope product expectations.
[05:29] Max: absolutely. pilot success criteria: 1) measured effective per-request cost within your target range, 2) p95 latency under 300ms, and 3) security checklist satisfied. If not, we'll explore options: smaller model TTR, more aggressive cache, or product scoping (rate limits, sampling).
[05:45] Rita: how long is pilot and what's Redwood provide?
[05:48] Sara: typically a 1-2 week perf pilot. Redwood will: run perf jobs with your prompts and traffic profile, produce token-level cost breakdown, advise batching/cache settings and propose dedicated reserved configurations if beneficial. we'll need your representative prompt set and traffic histogram.
[06:05] Liam: we can produce samples and the telemetry histogram. one more: what about quantization quality regression — we can't degrade driver safety text.
[06:13] Sara: important point. we have quant-aware evals and an eval harness to check hallucination/regression on your prompts. for safety-sensitive outputs we recommend running a baseline eval, and if quality drops with 4-bit quant, either stay on fp16 or use a validated quantization profile. part of the pilot is running those eval checks.
[06:31] Nina: for VPC peering and logs, can you confirm retention windows for audit logs? we have compliance needs for 90-days.
[06:38] Max: Redwood supports configurable log retention for enterprise customers — 90 days is typical on enterprise tiers, longer with archiving add-ons. we'll include that in the security pack.
[06:47] Tom: any competitor pitfalls we should watch for? we looked at CloudPrompt and OnyxServe — they advertised low per-token but hide cache hit assumptions and have longer latencies.
[06:56] Max: yeah, watch published per-token numbers vs effective cost after accounting for cache reuse, batching, and SLA. also verify model versions—some vendors use lighter models but with worse outputs. we'll help benchmark objectively.
[07:08] Sara: ok last part: logistics. Max will send pricing workbook with hosted/dedicated/private cost modeling and a recommended pilot config. Rita will share the prompt list and traffic histogram. we'll schedule the pilot kickoff next Tue 2026-04-06 and target results by 2026-04-17.
[07:25] Liam: sounds good. any other questions?
[07:28] Rita: none from me.
[07:29] Tom: just want the workbook to be explicit about committed vs on-demand assumptions.
[07:34] Max: will do. I'll include scenario lines: on-demand hosted, 3-month reserved dedicated, 12-month committed dedicated, and private amortization examples.
[07:43] Nina: I'll follow up once I read SOC2 doc; may have 1-2 technical q's on the KMS flow.
[07:48] Sara: perfect. we'll include a short diagram in the security pack showing BYOK flow.
[07:52] Max: thanks everyone — quick recap in chat with next steps and the links.
[07:56] Liam: thanks all.

End transcript.
